lawyer:
Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed with SM Manir, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
Md. Nurul Huq with ABM Khairul Hoque, AKM Shahidul Hoque and Miss Chaman Akhter, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Party Nos.l(1)-l(J).
parties:
Solaiman (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs
Sufia Akhtar Alam being dead, her heirs Narjesa Rahamatullah and others ----- Opposite party
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued at the instance of defendant No.1 of SCC Suit No.1 of 1982 against the plaintiff/opposite party No.1 calling upon her to show cause as to why the judgment and decree passed in that SCC suit should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts and circumstance which led to the filing of this revisional application under section 25 of the SCC Act in brief are as follows.

3. The plaintiff Sofia Akhter Alam (since deceased) filed the suit for a decree for ejectment of defendant No.1 from the suit shop claiming that the defendant No. 1 was a defaulter. Her case is that, her mother Rijia Khatoon was owner of the suit shop and the defendant No. 1 was a monthly tenant under her mother since 1st June, 1964. The plaintiff further claims that her mother orally gifted the ground floor of Holding No. 60/1, Purana Paltan to her on 29-8-77 and requested the monthly tenants both verbally and in writing to pay rent to the plaintiff instead of herself. In pursuance to that request, most of the tenants began to pay rent to the plaintiff but the defendant No.1 refused to accept the plaintiff as owner and continued to deposit rent before the House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 48 of 1972 in favour of her mother. The plaintiff wanted to start a handicraft business in the suit shop and requested the defendant to hand over vacant possession of the suit shop to her but he refused. Then a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served on 28-6-83 upon the defendant through Mr. KZM Faruqui requesting the defendant to vacate the possession by 31st July, 1983. The defendant, in spite of receiving the notice on 19-7-83, did not vacate the possession. The plaintiff then filed SCC Suit No. 91 of 1983 which was dismissed for default on 30-9-85. A Miscellaneous case was filed by the plaintiff which was also rejected. Then there was an attempt to settle the dispute amicably but that attempt also failed due to adamant attitude of the defendant. So, the plaintiff again served another notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 8-11-87 requesting the defendant to vacate possession by 30-11-87 but the defendant did not. The tenancy was terminated by the said notice and the defendant had no legal authority to remain in possession after termination of tenancy. Hence the suit.

4. The defendant No. 2, the mother of the plaintiff, appeared in the suit by filing a written statement and supported the case of the plaintiff by admitting that she gifted the suit shop to the plaintiff on 29-8-77. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations contained in the plaint. His case is that no notice of attornment was served upon him by either the plaintiff or her mother rather her mother continued to withdraw the amount of rent which he deposited in the court of the Rent Controller. He further claims that in 1973 Rijia Khatoon demanded rent at an exorbitant rate from him and, as such, he started depositing rent before the House Rent Controller by filing a case bearing No. 48 of 1973. Rijia Khatoon withdrew the house rent deposited before the House Rent Controller for the last time in December, 1986. The defendant further claims that as the plaintiff could not produce any legal proof that she got the suit shop from her mother on the basis of oral gift and, as such, in spite of their claim and demand, the defendant did not pay any rent to her and he continued to deposit the rent before the House Rent Controller in favour of her mother. The defendant also claims that no possession was delivered to the plaintiff on the basis of the alleged oral gift and no relationship of landlord and tenant was established at any time between him and the plaintiff. He paid rent although by way of deposit before House Rent Controller and was not defaulter. The plaintiff filed this false suit at the instance of her mother to evict him from the suit shop.

5. The learned trial Court, on consideration of the evidence on record, came to the finding that the defendant was although aware of the transfer of the suit shop in favour of the plaintiff by the original owner Rijia Khatoon and as he did not pay rent to the plaintiff in spite of demand, the defendant became a defaulter. The learned trial Court also found that though one month's notice was not given in pursuance of the original contract, as the suit was filed long after 30 days from the date of service of that notice, the notice was not insufficient. After coming to such findings, the learned trial Court decreed the suit.

6. The defendant No. 1 being aggrieved and dissatisfied by the judgment and decree of the trial Court, filed the present revisional application challenging the validity of the said judgment and decree mainly on two grounds, Firstly, the learned trial Court committed an error of law in holding the petitioner to be a defaulter because no notice of attornment was served upon the defendant/petitioner after the alleged oral gift in favour of the plaintiff by the original owner and that the original owner continued to withdraw the rent deposited before House Rent Controller in spite of such alleged oral gift. Secondly, in the original contract entered into between the defendant and Rijia Khatoon in 1964 it was stipulated that the tenancy could be determined only by one month's notice but though one month's notice was not served, the learned trial Court found that the notice served upon the defendant was sufficient.

7. At the time of hearing, arguments were addressed mainly on the two grounds as taken in the revisional application itself. Lengthy submissions have been made on behalf of Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner on the question that when there is any change of ownership, a notice of attornment upon the tenant is mandatory and without such notice a tenant is riot legally bound to pay rent to the new owner to whom ownership is transferred. In this connection, he referred to the statements made in the plaint and also the statement of the PWs to the effect that after the oral gift, Rijia Khatoon, the original owner and mother of the plaintiff in writing informed the tenants about the change in the ownership and or that, in fact, at the time of trial no such evidence could be led before the court to prove that there was any attornment.

8. As against the above submission of Mr. Khandakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Mr. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff/opposite party No. 1, submits that there is no provision either in the Transfer of Property Act or in any other law now in force about the requirement of serving a notice of attornment. According to him, knowledge of transfer of the ownership on the part of the tenant is sufficient. He contends that in the instant case the defendant was aware of the transfer of ownership from the very beginning and as he had knowledge regarding the change of the ownership, the defendant as a monthly tenant was legally bound to pay rent Ito the plaintiff. He had also submitted that even withdrawal of the house rent by the original owner cannot be a proof that there was no change of ownership and there was no gift. In this connection, he has pointed out that the rent which is deposited before the House Rent Controller would lapse if not withdrawn within 3 years from the date of deposit. Moreover, according to him, withdrawal of rent is not the same thing as acceptance of a person as a tenant.

9. As maximum emphasis has been given from the side of the petitioner on the question of service of attornment notice, I think it will be proper to discuss this question with reference to the facts and circumstances of the present suit. The plaintiff claims that the ground floor of the holding in question, including the suit shop was orally gifted to her by her mother on 29-8-77. It is also stated in paragraph 2 of the plaint that after the gift, the mother of the plaintiff informed in writing all the tenants about the gift and most of the tenants on getting such information, admitted the plaintiff to be the landlord. It has been argued that no such written notice could be proved by the plaintiff at the time oftrial. The learned trial Court discussed the evidence, both oral and documentary, of both parties and came to the conclusion that the defendant was aware of the gift in favour of the plaintiff from the time of gift Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed is of the view that a written notice is a must. On the other hand, Mr. Nurul Huq is of the view that knowledge of the change of ownership is sufficient. It is evident that the learned lower Court also gave emphasis on the fact that the defendant had knowledge regarding the change of the ownership.

<u>10. Now, let us see whether written notice is necessary or knowledge of the change of the ownership is sufficient. It appears that there is no provision or requirement of serving a notice of attornment after change of ownership. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed has also conceded that actually there is no provision for service of notice of attornment. With reference to the case of Madan Lal VS., Manakchand, reported in AIR 1971 (Rajasthan) 55, he has submitted that the word attornment has been borrowed from English law and has not been defined in any law of our country. In the said reported case it appears that both the original owner and the purchaser in writing informed the tenant about the transfer of ownership but I find nothing in the reported case to show that the service of any notice in writing is a legal requirement. The definition of the word attornment has been given by the court in the following words:</u>

<u>"It simply means an agreement or acknowledgement by a tenant that he holds the tenement of a new person as landlord."</u>

<u>In this case, the court also made the following observation.</u>

<u>"Such an agreement or attornment acts as an estoppel to prevent the tenant attorning from denying title of the one to whom he has attorned."</u>

<u>11. It is obvious that there is no provision in any law which requires service of any notice of attornment after change of any ownership. Even if there is no such provision, it is quite reasonable and it is also necessary that a tenant must know about the change of ownership. Unless he knows about the change of ownership, he will not be in a position to pay rent to the new owner and enter into a fresh agreement with the new owner. I cannot agree with the view that the information of the transfer must be made by serving a written notice. The purpose will be served if the tenant is informed both by the transferor and the transferees about the change of the ownership. It also appears that if the tenant has full knowledge of the change of the ownership by any other owners this knowledge should be sufficient for him to acknowledge the new owner as the landlord.</u>

12. Now, let us see whether the defendant had knowledge of the change of the ownership. I have already mentioned that the trial Court came to a finding on the basis of the evidence on record that the defendant had such a knowledge. The plaintiff's case is that the defendant was informed of the change of ownership both in writing and verbally. It is true that the plaintiff could not produce the copy of such notice at the time of trial but most of the PWs categorically stated that defendant was informed about the change of the ownership both in writing and verbally. PW I stated this in her examination-in-chief. PW 2 who is the younger brother of the plaintiff, has stated as follows.

১৯৭৭ সালে মৌখিক দানপত্র করিয়া দিবার পর মাতা ভাড়াটিয়াদের জানাইয়া দেয় এখন হইতে মালিকবাদীনি এবং সেই মর্মে লিখিতভাবে জানাইয়া দেয়া হয় তখন আমরা সকল ভাইবোনেরা উপস্থিত ছিলাম।ভাড়াটিয়াদের লিখিতভাবেও নোটিশ প্রদান করা হইয়াছিল এবং উক্ত নোটিশের কপি এডভোকেট এ,জি, ফারুখী সাহেবের নিকট হইতে missing হইয়া গিয়াছে।

Mother of the plaintiff deposes as DW 4. Her statement is as follows"

আমি সব দোকানদারদের জানাইয়াছি যে, আমার মেয়ে বাদীনি নালিশী দোকানের মালিক। আমি নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে আমার মেয়েকে দেওয়ার পরে কেউ মেনে নিয়েছে এবং কেউ মেয়ে নেয়নাই। যাহারা মেনে নাই বাদীনিকে মালিক হিসাব তাহাদেরকে আমি মালিক হিসাবে জানাইয়াছি।

13. Defendant No.1 as DW 1 admitted that some of the tenants started to pay rent to the plaintiff as there was change of ownership. This statement is made in his examination-in-cross which is as follows:

"নিপ্পন টেড্রার্স এবং সাইদি গ্লাসহাউস এবং দুইটি ভাড়াটিয়া বাদীনির বরাবরে ভাড়া দিতেছে। কারণ পূর্বের মালিক হাত বদলাইয়াছে।”

This is a clear admission on the part of the defendant No. 1 that there was change of the ownership and for that reason some of the original tenants started paying monthly rent to the plaintiff. The above statement also supports the case of the plaintiff that when the monthly tenants were informed about the change of the ownership by both the original owner and the present plaintiff, some of them accepted the plaintiff as the new landlord and others including the defendant No. 1 did not There is no earthly reason to believe that the plaintiff and her mother informed about change of the ownership only to the Nippon Traders and Saidi-Glass House and did not inform the other three tenants including the defendant No. 1. The trial Court, with reference to the entire evidence on record, came to a definite finding that the defendant No. 1 had knowledge of the change of the ownership since 1977. From the evidence on record and from the statements of the DW 1 as quoted above, I am also convinced that defendant No. 1 was fully aware of the change of the ownership from the time of the transfer of the suit shop to the plaintiff by way of oral gift. It appears that the defendant resisted the claim of the plaintiff under some mis-conceptions. He stated as DW 1 that he did not receive any attornment notice but at the same time he also stated that he was bound to pay rent to the plaintiff if she was the owner. I do not understand how he could deny the title of the plaintiff only because he received no attornment notice. When he had full knowledge of the change of the ownership, he was bound to pay rent to the new owner. There is no law requiring service of attornment notice nor there is any specific form for such a notice prescribed by any law. Under such circumstances, the defendant No. 1 cannot deny the ownership of the plaintiff. Had there been a legal requirement of serving such a notice, the defendant could have some justification for denying the ownership of the plaintiff. In view of the above position and evidence on record, I am of the opinion that the learned lower court committed no error of law in holding that the defendant had knowledge of the change in the ownership in favour of the plaintiff and, as such, the defendant was legally bound to pay rent to the plaintiff.

14. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed has also contended that the transfer being a normal gift, the ownership will devolve only when possession is delivered by the donor in favour of the donee instantaneously. He has further submitted that the original owner Rijia Khatoon withdrew the rent which the defendant deposited before the House Rent Controller. With reference Exhibit (II), he has also argued that the suit shop was shown to be the property of Rijia Khatoon in the Income-tax Return filed by Rijia Khatoon for the year 1987-88. So, according to him, there was no oral gift as claimed by the plaintiff. As against these submissions, Mr. Nurul Hoq, the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party, has submitted that a gift is complete when a donee accepts it and possession is delivered. According to him, the gift in favour of the plaintiff will not become invalid even if the property is shown in the Income-tax return of the donor as her own property.

15. In this case the gift has been made by a mother in favour of a daughter. For an oral gift, the legal requirements are that there must be an offer and acceptance and there must be also delivery of possession in favour of the donee. In the instant case, the property gifted was in possession of the monthly tenants. So, the question of handing over physical possession of the property does not arise. In such a case, it will be sufficient if the tenants in possession are informed of the gift by the owner and are requested to pay rent to the donee. I have found that such information was given and request was made.

16.The present defendant was a monthly tenant under the original owner Rijia Khatoon. He is not legally competent to challenge the gift itself. Mr. Nurul Huq while making his submissions invited my attention to the fact that the donor Rijia Khatoon appeared in the present suit and admitted that she made an oral gift in favour of the plaintiff in 1977 and also delivered possession by requesting the monthly tenants to pay rent to the plaintiff instead of herself. Mr. Nurul Huq also cited the case of Fatal Ahmed vs. Rakhi reported in PLD (Lahore) 218. The donor in the reported case also appeared by filing written statement and admitted that gift. I have been take through the relevant observation of the court as made in paragraph 13 which is reproduced below:

"13. In the present case, the rule of Muhammadan Law as to delivery of possession is not being violated if we have regard to the reason of this rule. Here, the donor has supported the gift and not only has he filed a written statement admitting the claim of the plaintiff and praying that a decree be passed in his favour but he has appeared in the witness box.........."

Hence, in the instant case also, I find that the donor Rijia Khatoon, appeared by filing written statement and also deposed before the court in support of the claim of the plaintiff and categorically stated that she made oral gift in 1977. The defendant's status is that of a monthly tenant and he not being a claimant of title in the property through the donor and not being a co-sharer in the property through the donor, cannot challenge the validity of the gift. His only right as tenant is that he should be informed of the transfer. We have found that he was informed of the transfer and he had full knowledge of the transfer. Similar decision was also given by the trial Court in the impugned judgment, I find that the learned lower court was not wrong in arriving at such a decision.

<u>17. Another ground on which the validity of the impugned judgment and decree has been challenged is that of insufficiency of the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The notice was issued on 8-11-87 asking the defendant No. 1 to vacate the possession on 30-11-87 on. So, it is obvious that one month's notice as stipulated under the original agreement of 1964 was not served. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed is of the view that when clear one month's time was not given by the said notice, the relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant as landlord and tenant cannot be severed and terminated. Mr. Nurul Huq, on the other hand, has submitted that the suit was filed after expiry of 57 days from the date of issue of the notice and, as such, the notice cannot be considered to be insufficient. He is also of the view that the defendant refused to accept the plaintiff as landlord even after he came to know about the change in the ownership and by this denial, the defendant forfeited his right and as a tenant and, as such, even without a notice. The plaintiff can come with a suit for ejectment. Mr. Nurul Huq, in support of his view referred to the case of Maulvi Paiz Bakhsh vs. Syed Shadi Shah reported in PW 1956 (Lahore) 261. It appears that the learned trial Court also found that though clear one month's notice was not issue the suit was filed long after one month from the date of the issue of the notice. In the case cited above, notice was given on 3rd August, 1954 and received by the tenant on 8th August, 1954 and the suit having been instituted on 13th November, 1954, it was held that the suit for ejectment having been filed after 3 months' notice, the defendant was not prejudiced merely because the period mentioned in the notice did not expire with the last date of the month of the tenancy. The principle laid down in this cited case appears to be applicable in the present Case before us and the learned trial Court has actually applied this principle.</u>

18. About the question relating to service of notice under section 106 of the TP Act, Mr. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate on behalf of the plaintiff, has submitted that the original contract between Rajia Khatoon and defendant No. 1 was no longer in force because that was a contract between Rajia Khatoon and the defendant No. 1 and not between Rijia Khatoon and Greenland and Company. In this connection he has also referred to the statement of DW 1 which he made in his examination-in-cross to the effect that the tenancy which was created in 1964 came to an end in 1970 when the defendant No. 1 created a new partnership firm in the name and style of Greenland and Co. in the year 1970. Mr. Huq is also of the view that when the original tenancy came to an end in 1970, the original contractual obligation of serving one month's notice was also not in force. I think there is much substance in this argument. When the defendant No. 1 entered into a contract of tenancy with Rijia Khatoon in 1964, the contract was not with the firm Greenland and Company. The defendant No. 1 entered into the contract in his individual capacity. The status changed when the defendant started a new business firm in the year 1970 in the name and style of Greenland and Company. Rijia Khatoon accepted rent from this new firm Greenland and Company arid it is evident that rent receipts were issued by her in favour of the Greenland and Company. From all these, it appears that fresh tenancy was created and, as such, it cannot be said that the original contract of 1964 was in force. In view of this position, it also cannot be said that one month's notice would be necessary for determination of the fresh or new tenancy. The fresh tenancy was created without any written contract. So, 15 days notice as provided under section 106 of the TP Act will be sufficient.

19. From the above we have found that the defendant No. 1 was informed of the change of the ownership and he had knowledge about transfer of the suit shop to the plaintiff by the original owner. In spite of this knowledge, the defendant denied the title of the plaintiff and refused to accept her as the new owner. It is admitted by both the parties that this denial was made after the gift Admittedly two of the tenants at that time accepted the plaintiff as owner or new landlord and started paying rent to her but the present defendant and two other tenants refused to accept the plaintiff as landlord. It has been settled in so many cases by superior courts of this sub-continent that denial of the title of the owner by the tenant itself will be sufficient for the purpose of obviating the necessity of any notice to vacate. Mr. Huq in this connection also referred to the case of Muhammad Islam Khan vs. Cantonment Board, reported in 1982 Supreme Court Monthly Review, 1056. In this reported case it has been held that the defendant's denial of the plaintiff's title in property can operate as forfeiture and dispense with the notice under section 106 of the TP Act.

20. Considering the entire legal position I am of the opinion that as regards the present suit, the ground of insufficiency of the notice under section 106 of the TP Act as taken by the petitioner cannot be tenable and the notice as given by the plaintiff to the defendant under the above section may be considered as sufficient.

21. Thus in view of the above discussion and on consideration of the evidence, facts, circumstance and the legal position, I find no reason to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by the learned SCC Court.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the learned SCC Judge be affirmed.

End.
